title: Together, lives on
hookLine: an old couple, Nakula's parents, wish to meet again in future lives: shared faith, virtue, giving, wisdom

cards: These two are not monks or nuns. They're an old married couple from the Bhagga country, known in the texts as Nakula's father and Nakula's mother, married young.
One day they come to the Buddha together, and the husband says something remarkable for any marriage, ancient or modern.
Since she was brought to me as a girl, he says, I don't know of ever having been unfaithful to her, not even in thought. And his wife says the same of him. Then they ask for something bigger.

teach.h: MEET AGAIN IN LIVES TO COME.
teach.b: We want to see each other not only in this life, but in lives to come. Is there a way? In the Buddhist picture, life doesn't end at one death; beings are carried from life to life by what they've done and become.
So the couple's question is a real one, and the Buddha takes it seriously. Yes, he says. If a husband and wife both wish to see each other in this life and the next, let them be equal in four things.
Equal in faith, the trust that sets you on the path. Equal in virtue, the way you keep your conduct. Equal in generosity, the open hand.

Equal in wisdom, seeing how things really are. If those four are shared, they will see each other in this life and in the life to come. Notice what's not on the list: not looks, not money, not even shared tastes in food.
The bond he points to is a shared practice, two people walking the same way at the same pace, and it's a list you can work on together.
Elsewhere in the Numbered Sayings, the Buddha names Nakula's father and mother as foremost among his lay followers in one quality: trust, the kind of closeness people can lean on.
An honor shared by a husband and wife, and a happy marriage held up as a model.

how: Buddhist teachers draw on the story of Nakula's parents in talks on marriage, and some Buddhist couples practice together by keeping the precepts, giving, and going to the temple as a family.

games.why: he gives them four things to share. the answer isn't a vow or a farewell, but a practice they can do together.

practice: Bring to mind someone close, a partner, a parent, a friend, a sibling, and picture their face.
Go gently through the four: something you both trust in, a way of behaving you both care about, a way you both like to give, something you've both come to understand.
Rest with whichever one you share most, and let a little gratitude for it in.

wordCard.voice: Together. Nakula's parents, the old couple of the Numbered Sayings, and the four things the Buddha said keep two lives side by side: faith, virtue, giving and wisdom, shared. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali samasaddha: 'of the same faith,' the first of four; the sutta goes on: same virtue, same giving, same wisdom.

carryVoice: Your line: side by side. Faith, virtue, giving and wisdom, shared, and two lives keep walking together. Day six hundred sixty-four.
